card.title: Elastic modulus: Young modulus, bulk modulus, shear modulus

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: The three elastic moduli — Young's (E), bulk (B), and shear (G) — quantify how materials resist stretching, uniform compression, and shape change respectively. Each is stress/strain with units N/m². They are related by E = 2G(1+σ) = 3B(1−2σ). Solids possess all three; fluids have only bulk modulus.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Y = FL/(A ΔL)
K = −P/(ΔV/V)
U = ½kx²

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Material State Determines Available Moduli:** Solids have all three moduli ($E, B, G$). Fluids (liquids/gases) have *only* bulk modulus $B$ — they cannot sustain shear stress ($G=0$) and have no defined Young's modulus for stretching.  ·  **Isotropic Material Relations:** For isotropic solids, the three moduli are linked via Poisson's ratio $\sigma$: $E = 2G(1+\sigma) = 3B(1-2\sigma)$. These relations *do not hold* for anisotropic materials (crystals, composites) where moduli depend on direction.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Choose the modulus by the type of deformation: stretch → E, squeeze → B, twist → G.  ·  The sign in B = −P/(ΔV/V) makes the modulus positive since ΔV is negative under compression.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Worked: identify given → pick sub-concept → apply standard form → check units / edges.  ·  Young: A 1 mm² wire, 2 m long, carrying 200 N extends 2 mm → E = (200/10⁻⁶)/(2×10⁻³/2) = 2×10¹¹ N/m².

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Covers only: elastic modulus, young modulus, bulk modulus, shear modulus (within Elasticity).  ·  Out of scope here: topics of neighbouring units in Physics — don't mix them.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Compute Young's modulus from a wire experiment data set.  ·  Compute bulk modulus from a known pressure and volume change.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: unit memory: all three moduli are in N/m² (Pa).  ·  For Young's modulus: rearrange E = Fl/(AΔl) to solve any one variable.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Young's modulus E = Fl/(AΔl) describes stretching/compression stiffness.  ·  Bulk modulus B = −P/(ΔV/V) describes compression under uniform pressure.  ·  Shear modulus G = τ/θ describes change of shape under tangential stress.  ·  The three moduli are interrelated: E = 2G(1+σ) = 3B(1−2σ).

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: • Elastic modulus  ·  • Young modulus  ·  • Bulk modulus  ·  • Shear modulus

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Stress = F/A, strain = ΔL/L (dimensionless). Hooke's law (elastic limit): stress ∝ strain.  ·  Elastic moduli: Young's Y = (F/A)/(ΔL/L); Bulk K = −P/(ΔV/V); Shear G = (F/A)/(Δx/L).

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: solve / apply for "Elastic modulus: Young modulus, bulk modulus, shear modulus" and verify the answer is plausible.  ·  A 2 m copper wire of area 1 mm² extends by 1.2 mm under a 40 N load. Find Young's modulus for copper.  ·  Calculate the bulk modulus of a liquid if 2×10⁶ Pa pressure reduces 1.5 m³ of it by 0.75×10⁻³ m³.

rows.label: More hints
rows.text: The relation E = 2G(1+σ) is frequently used to find Poisson's ratio.  ·  Comparing bulk moduli of solids, liquids, gases comes up in conceptual questions.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: Bulk: 3×10⁶ Pa pressure shrinks 1 m³ of steel by 1.9×10⁻⁵ m³ → B = 1.6×10¹¹ Pa.  ·  Shear: A 2×10⁴ N force shears a 10⁻³ m² face by 2.5×10⁻³ rad → G = (2×10⁴/10⁻³)/2.5×10⁻³ = 8×10⁹ N/m².

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: Young's modulus is the ratio of longitudinal stress to: → C  ·  A liquid has which elastic modulus? → C

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Stress and strain.** Stress is the restoring force per unit area (F/A) and strain is the fractional deformation (ΔL/L); within the elastic limit, stress is proportional to strain (Hooke's law).  ·  **Young's modulus.** Y = longitudinal stress ÷ longitudinal strain = FL/AΔL; it measures a material's resistance to stretching or compression along its length.  ·  **Bulk modulus.** K = −P ÷ (ΔV/V); the negative sign shows volume decreases under pressure, and its reciprocal is the compressibility of the material.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Fluids possess only bulk modulus; compressibility = 1/B.  ·  Young's modulus: E = (F/A)/(Δl/l) = Fl/(AΔl)  ·  Bulk modulus: B = −P/(ΔV/V)

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Shear modulus: G = (F/A)/θ = τ/θ  ·  Relation: E = 2G(1 + σ) = 3B(1 − 2σ)  ·  Combined: E = 9BG/(3B + G); compressibility k = 1/B

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Geometry Separation:** $E$ is an intensive material property (Pa), while spring constant $k = EA/L$ is extensive. Changing a wire's length or cross-section changes $k$ but not $E$ — this distinction is essential for connecting spring problems to material science.  ·  E, B, G all have units N/m² (Pa) — they differ by the type of deformation they describe.  ·  E (stretching), B (volume), G (shape) measure the corresponding resistance of a material.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: The three moduli are linked: E = 2G(1+σ) and E = 3B(1−2σ).  ·  Liquids and gases have G = 0 (they cannot resist shear) — only solids have a shear modulus.  ·  Compressibility is the reciprocal of B.
